extracted.intended_audience: the people of New York; voters, policymakers, and delegates considering ratification of the U.S. Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic exposition of the powers conferred on the federal government and the restrictions imposed on the states by the proposed U.S. Constitution, with justificatory commentary and examples. Written to inform citizens and legislators deciding on ratification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-class federal powers (harmony among the States)
rubrics_metrics.description: Powers which provide for the harmony and proper intercourse among the States: to regulate commerce among the several States and the Indian tribes; to coin money, regulate the value thereof, and of foreign coin; to provide for the punishment of counterfeiting the current coin and securities of the United States; to fix the standard of weights and measures; to establish a uniform rule of naturalization, and uniform laws of bankruptcy; to prescribe the manner in which the public acts, records, and judicial proceedings of each State shall be proved, and the effect they shall have in other States; and to establish post offices and post roads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justification and explanatory remarks: without a national authority to regulate interstate commerce, individual States could tax or burden goods in transit, producing animosities and interruptions to public tranquility (examples: Switzerland, Germany, Netherlands). Regulation of commerce with Indian tribes must avoid the Confederation's contradictory limitations. Uniformity in the VALUE of coin (including foreign coin) is necessary; the power to punish counterfeiting extends to public securities; uniform weights and measures and uniform naturalization rules prevent conflicting local laws that would produce legal and political confusion (examples of adverse consequences of differing naturalization rules are given). Uniform bankruptcy laws prevent fraud when parties or property move among States. Prescribing how public acts/records/judicial proceedings are proved and recognized in other States is a practical instrument of justice, especially near borders. Establishing post offices and post roads is a benign power that can produce public convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to promote progress of science and useful arts (copyrights and patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: A power 'to promote the progress of science and useful arts, by securing, for a limited time, to authors and inventors, the exclusive right to their respective writings and discoveries.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility: author and inventor rights align with public good; States cannot separately make effective provisions for this. Many States have already enacted such laws at Congress's instance; a national power avoids fragmentation and secures incentives for creativity and invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive legislation over federal district and places purchased for forts etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: Power 'to exercise exclusive legislation, in all cases whatsoever, over such district (not exceeding ten miles square) as may, by cession of particular States and the acceptance of Congress, become the seat of the government of the United States; and to exercise like authority over all places purchased by the consent of the legislatures of the States in which the same shall be, for the erection of forts, magazines, arsenals, dockyards, and other needful buildings.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Necessity: complete authority at the seat of government prevents insult or interruption to public authority; prevents dependence of federal officers on the State for protection; accumulated public improvements would be insecure under single-State control. Objections obviated by limiting extent, requiring state consent to cede, allowing municipal/local self-government for inhabitants, and deriving concurrence from the people via ratification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to declare punishment of treason with limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Power 'to declare the punishment of treason, but no attainder of treason shall work corruption of blood, or forfeiture, except during the life of the person attained.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: As treason can be committed against the United States, federal authority must be able to punish it. Safeguards: the Constitution defines the crime, fixes the proof necessary for conviction, and restrains Congress from extending consequences beyond the offender (e.g., no corruption of blood). This guards against abuses of treason charges as instruments of faction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to admit new States with procedural safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Power 'to admit new States into the Union; but no new State shall be formed or erected within the jurisdiction of any other State; nor any State be formed by the junction of two or more States, or parts of States, without the consent of the legislatures of the States concerned, as well as of the Congress.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fills a Confederation omission. The provision prevents creation of new States inside existing States or by partition without the State's consent (quiets jealousy of large states) and prevents forced junctions (protects smaller states). Congress plus affected states must concur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to dispose of and regulate United States territories and property
rubrics_metrics.description: Power 'to dispose of and make all needful rules and regulations respecting the territory or other property belonging to the United States, with a proviso, that nothing in the Constitution shall be so construed as to prejudice any claims of the United States, or of any particular State.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important for managing national lands and property; the proviso is to avoid prejudicing existing claims and to address jealousies/questions over Western territory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guarantee of republican government and protection against invasion/domestic violence
rubrics_metrics.description: Power 'to guarantee to every State in the Union a republican form of government; to protect each of them against invasion; and on application of the legislature, or of the executive (when the legislature cannot be convened), against domestic violence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: to defend the confederate republican system against aristocratic/monarchical innovations and to preserve forms substantially. The guaranty is limited: it secures pre-existing republican forms; States may change to other republican forms and claim guaranty. Protection against invasion and mutual aid against domestic violence is appropriate, with reference to historical confederacies (Swiss example). Federal interposition is generally a preventive remedy and may be required where local authority cannot cope or where violence threatens federal-linked constitutional structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of pre-constitution debts and obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Power 'to consider all debts contracted, and engagements entered into, before the adoption of this Constitution, as being no less valid against the United States, under this Constitution, than under the Confederation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declaratory function to reassure foreign creditors and uphold moral obligations; insertion aimed to dispel fears that a change in political form dissolves prior obligations. The clause is defensive against critics who allege the federal government might repudiate debts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to provide for constitutional amendments (three-fourths rule with exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Power 'to provide for amendments to be ratified by three fourths of the States under two exceptions only.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: balances adaptability and stability—guards against excessive mutability and excessive rigidness. The exceptions (e.g., equality of suffrage in the Senate) protect fundamental structural bargains that secure residuary sovereignty of the States; the amendment mode enables corrections suggested by experience from either federal or state governments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratification by nine states sufficient to establish the Constitution among ratifying states
rubrics_metrics.description: Provision: 'The ratification of the conventions of nine States shall be sufficient for the establishment of this Constitution between the States, ratifying the same.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: requiring unanimity would enable a single State to frustrate essential interests of all. The people (not solely legislatures) provide the express authority. The proviso addresses delicate questions about how the Confederation may be superseded and what relation dissenting states bear to ratifiers; moral duties remain though political relations differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibitions on States (no treaties, prizes, coinage, paper money, bills of attainder/ex post facto, titles of nobility, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clause: 'No State shall enter into any treaty, alliance, or confederation; grant letters of marque and reprisal; coin money; emit bills of credit; make any thing but gold and silver a legal tender in payment of debts; pass any bill of attainder, ex-post-facto law, or law impairing the obligation of contracts; or grant any title of nobility.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: continuity with Confederation on forbidding treaties; extending prohibition on letters of marque to peacetime preserves uniform foreign policy responsibility. Coinage and paper money powers are removed to prevent multiplicity of currencies and the pernicious effects of paper money on confidence, industry, morals, and republican stability. Bills of attainder, ex post facto laws, and laws impairing contracts violate social compact principles; prohibition is a constitutional bulwark for personal security and private rights. Titles of nobility prohibition is retained without comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Further state restraints (consent of Congress required for imposts, tonnage duties, standing troops/ships, compacts, war)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clause: 'No State shall, without the consent of the Congress, lay any imposts or duties on imports or exports, except what may be absolutely necessary for executing its inspection laws, and the net produce of all duties and imposts laid by any State on imports or exports, shall be for the use of the treasury of the United States; and all such laws shall be subject to the revision and control of the Congress. No State shall, without the consent of Congress, lay any duty on tonnage, keep troops or ships of war in time of peace, enter into any agreement or compact with another State, or with a foreign power, or engage in war unless actually invaded, or in such imminent danger as will not admit of delay.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: restraints on states' power over imports/exports enforce a uniform national trade policy and avoid inter-state imposts that would disrupt commerce; net proceeds are for the federal treasury and subject to Congress review. Prohibitions on tonnage duties, maintaining peacetime troops/ships, and making compacts or engaging in war without federal consent protect national security and avoid conflicting foreign or inter-state entanglements.
